newsitem.title: USA: Group cautions housing issuers on muni disclosure.
newsitem.headline: Group cautions housing issuers on muni disclosure.

text.p: With federal scrutiny of muni market disclosure on the rise, housing bond issuers must take steps now to guard against enforcement action, a group representing housing agencies warned Wednesday.

"Be careful out there!" the Association of Local Housing Finance Agencies (ALHFA) warned in draft guidelines to be mailed to ALHFA members next month on how to avoid liability under the Securities and Exchange Commission's municipal disclosure and antifraud standards.
"Do not panic or let real or imagined fear about liability keep you from fulfilling (your) public purpose," the group said.
But agency boards and staffs can follow certain steps to head off legal problems in the "complicated" world of housing bonds, the group said.

Federal securities laws and regulations bar housing agencies from misrepresenting or omitting "material" facts when selling tax-exempt bonds and other securities. Violators can be fined, disbarred or subject to other penalities.

In addition, SEC's muni disclosure Rule 15c2-12 bars broker-dealers from underwriting bonds unless issuers pledge in writing to provide ongoing disclosure of annual financial information and material events.

ALFHA said the standards are "all the more complicated in the world of housing bonds" where authorities often serve as "conduits" for private companies and issue bonds so infrequently that they hire no technical staff.
Nevertheless, increased regulation means housing agency boards and staffs need to take to take certain steps now, ALFHA said.

ALFHA "strongly" recommended that boards hire at least part-time staff who understand rental housing or mortgage loan programs, cash flow expectations and risk factors, the draft said. That is so staff can educate board members on material information, ALFHA said.
And each issuer must have a regulator financial advisor who is independent of the underwriter and a public finance lawyer, ALFHA said.
Boards should educate themselves about housing bonds, new financing techniques, and local real estate developments. Or they should fill vacancies with someone knowledgeable.
But board members should not take on official responsibilities of staff and professionals because they may "unwittingly" take on liability, ALHFA said.

In other recommendations, ALHFA said board staff should read all bond documents, keep a standard list of questions for parties to each financing, keep complete board meeting records, and give board members time to review draft official statements.

ALHFA said board members can "reasonably" rely on consultants' advice, but not accept blanket opinions. Documents should disclose any conflicts of interest with consultants, such as political contributions, ALFHA said.
One section of the document asks, "Is ignorance a defense against fraud allegations?"
ALHFA says, "In conduit financings, the issuer may be protected if it can show that it undertook all reasonable actions to check the accuracy of statements made by the borrower."

Board members and staff are not expected to have "supernatural insight" into the future success of a project, ALHFA said. "Rather, the board and/or staff should have in place procedures to investigate material information."

ALHFA said boards need not second guess financial statements audited by licensed CPAs. "If they have not been audited, board members should insist that staff review and feel comfortable with the numbers," ALHFA said.

The guidelines were prepared by Sara Oberlies, ALHFA's housing finance director, and bond lawyers John Wagner of Kutak Rock and Richard Martin of Leonard, Street and Deinard. SEC "provided input," according to the document.
--Vicky Stamas, U.S. Municipals Desk, 202-898--8314
